'''''Salvia leucophylla''''', the '''San Luis purple sage'''<ref>{{PLANTS|id=SALE3|taxon=Salvia leucophylla|access-date=28 October 2015}}</ref> or '''gray sage''', is an [[aroma compound|aromatic]] [[Salvia|sage]] native to the southern coastal mountain ranges of [[the Californias]].

==Description==
[[File:IMG 0438-Salvia leucophylla.jpg|thumb|Foliage]]

''S. leucophylla'' is an [[evergreen]] shrub that grows up to {{convert|1|to|1.5|m|ft|abbr=off|frac=2}} tall and wide. The [[leaves]] are a light green in the spring, turning grayish-white as they mature, with graceful branches that arch to the ground, sometimes rooting when they touch the ground. Flowers grow in tight whorls on {{convert|15|to|20|cm|in|abbr=off|frac=2}} long inflorescences, with a pinkish-purple flowering stem. The {{convert|2.5|cm|in|abbr=on|frac=4}} flowers are pinkish-purple, held in a purple-tinged gray [[Sepal|calyx]].<ref name="Clebsch">{{cite book |last1=Clebsch |first1=Betsy |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=NM0iwB8GrQYC&pg=PA174 |title=The New Book of Salvias |last2=Barner |first2=Carol D. |publisher=Timber Press |year=2003 |isbn=978-0-88192-560-9 |pages=174–176}}</ref>

== Taxonomy ==
The plant's [[specific epithet]], ''leucophylla'', describes the light grayish leaves. The [[type specimen]] was collected near [[Santa Barbara, California]], by Scottish botanist [[David Douglas (botanist)|David Douglas]] and named by [[Edward Lee Greene]] in 1892. The common names refer to the pale purple flowers (purple sage) or to the grayish leaves (gray sage).<ref name="Clebsch" />

== Distribution and habitat ==
The plant is native to the southern coastal mountain ranges of [[California]] and [[Baja California]],<ref name="Clebsch" /> typically being found on dry hillsides and in gravelly soils.<ref name="Clebsch" />

==Cultivation==
The species is widely used in California and xeriscape gardening, preferring full sun and good drainage. There are many [[cultivar]]s, natural [[Hybrid (biology)|hybrids]], and wild hybrids with other ''Salvia'' species, making clear naming very confusing.

Some cultivars include:
*''Salvia leucophylla'' 'Pt. Sal'
*''Salvia leucophylla'' 'Figueroa'
*''Salvia leucophylla'' 'Bee's Bliss'<ref name="Clebsch" />

''Salvia leucophylla'' is known to have [[allelopathic]] qualities. It is thought that [[monoterpenoids]] released from the plant may be responsible for inhibiting the growth of neighboring seedlings.<ref>{{cite book |last=McClure |first=Susan |year=1994 |title=Companion Planting |publisher=Rodale Press |isbn=0-87596-616-0 |url-access=registration |url=https://archive.org/details/companionplantin0000mccl }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal| doi = 10.1007/s10886-005-4256-y| issn = 1573-1561| volume = 31| issue = 5| pages = 1187–1203| last1 = Nishida| first1 = Nami| last2 = Tamotsu| first2 = Satoshi| last3 = Nagata| first3 = Noriko| last4 = Saito| first4 = Chieko| last5 = Sakai| first5 = Atsushi| title = Allelopathic Effects of Volatile Monoterpenoids Produced by Salvia leucophylla: Inhibition of Cell Proliferation and DNA Synthesis in the Root Apical Meristem of Brassica campestris Seedlings| journal = Journal of Chemical Ecology| access-date = 2020-11-29| date = 2005-05-01| pmid = 16124241| bibcode = 2005JCEco..31.1187N| s2cid = 20650192| url = https://doi.org/10.1007/s10886-005-4256-y| url-access = subscription}}</ref>
